results.summary: This design implements an 8-bit shift register with output latches, functionally equivalent to the 74HC595. It accepts serial data and control signals (sclrn, ser, rck, srck, G) and provides 8 parallel outputs. External hardware required includes 8 LEDs or a PMOD LED module. The design has been tested with a bit-banging program to create a Knight Rider effect, confirming it works on silicon.

This design implements the NIST 800.22 Monobit test for evaluating the randomness of a bit source. It takes one bit per clock cycle and outputs a valid signal and an is_random flag every 65536 cycles. No external hardware is required for operation. The design is an HLS implementation and is intended for testing random number generators.

This design plays the Super Mario tune on a piezo speaker using differential PWM modulation. It requires a 3125 Hz clock and a piezo speaker connected across the two output pins. The design converts an RTTL ringtone into Verilog using Python. It has been tested and works on silicon.

This design converts an 8-bit binary input into signals to drive a 7-segment display showing hexadecimal digits. It takes 8 input bits and outputs 8 bits for the 7-segment segments and decimal point. External hardware required is a 7-segment display. The documentation is minimal, with placeholder text for how it works and how to test.

This design is a RISC-V CPU called LaRVa with a serial port, JTAG interface, and a few peripherals. It requires external SRAM memory and address latches attached to PMOD connectors for full operation. A bootloader allows programs to be loaded via the serial port at 115200 bps. The design has been tested by sending an 'L' character and receiving a reply.

This design implements a 4-bit successive approximation analog-to-digital converter (ADC). It requires an external sample-and-hold circuit to keep the analog input constant during conversion. The conversion takes 5 clock cycles at 5 MHz, yielding a 1 MHz conversion rate. The digital output is available on four pins along with an end-of-conversion signal.

This design is a simple one-stage RISC-V CPU based on a university lecture. Instructions are 32-bit but loaded over four clock cycles via an 8-bit input bus. The CPU outputs the ALU result on 8 output pins. The design has been tested with simple instructions in a testbench, but the chip is not being shipped.

This design is a factory test module that either mirrors inputs to outputs or outputs a counter depending on a select pin. When input 0 is high, a counter is output on all output and bidirectional pins; otherwise, inputs are passed through. No external hardware is required. The test is performed by setting input 0 high and checking that outputs toggle.

This design implements an 8-bit Concurrent Built-In Logic Block Observer (CBILBO) for memory testing. It uses D flip-flops, multiplexers, and logic gates to shift and feedback data. No external hardware is required. The design is intended for built-in self-test applications and has been simulated but not reported as tested on silicon.

This design outputs a user-selectable Latin character on a 7-segment display. Six DIP switches select the character from a set of 32 (letters, space, underscore, dash, dot, exclamation, double quote). A high clock rate is required because the display is driven one segment at a time. Silicon test reports confirm it works as intended.
